title: Association between prenatal glucocorticoid exposure and adolescent neurodevelopment: An observational follow-up study.
ehr_evidence: Data were collected prospectively through in-person clinical assessments (RIAS IQ test, EEG, salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase, ECG/heart rate variability, TSST stress test) and parent questionnaires; pregnancy and birth data were obtained from hospital records or the German maternity passport, and the reference group was selected from medical birth records.
summary: A prospective observational follow-up study of 21 betamethasone-exposed and 35 unexposed 14- to 15-year-old adolescents assessed whether prenatal glucocorticoid exposure was associated with cognitive performance (IQ), ADHD symptoms, metabolic markers, and neurophysiological outcomes.
key_findings: No statistically significant difference in global IQ between betamethasone and reference groups (adjusted mean difference −2.0, 95% CI: −7.12 to 3.12, p = 0.44).
No statistically significant differences in ADHD core symptoms, BMI, or HOMA-IR (insulin resistance) between groups.
No statistically significant differences in HPAA (salivary cortisol) or autonomic nervous system activity during the stress test.
Betamethasone-exposed adolescents exhibited reduced frontal electrocortical activity (spectral edge frequency 16.0 Hz vs 17.8 Hz, mean difference −1.83 Hz, 95% CI: −3.21 to −0.45, p = 0.01).
captured_features: RIAS composite IQ and verbal/non-verbal subscale scores
Heart rate variability (mean heart rate, LF/HF band power)
EEG spectral edge frequency (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital)
Socioeconomic status and Zurich Life-Event List scores
population: 21 betamethasone-exposed and 35 unexposed 14- to 15-year-old adolescents born near term with weight appropriate for gestational age, recruited from Jena and Gera, Germany
exposure_domain: Prenatal glucocorticoid (betamethasone) exposure for fetal lung maturation
limitations: Small sample size and reduced statistical power risking a type II error.
Selection bias from selective participation and loss of follow-up, particularly among children with extreme IQ scores.
Potential residual confounding and inability to establish causality due to the observational design.
No adjustment for multiple comparisons raising false-positive risk.
Maternal psychosocial stress associated with preterm birth may have modified outcomes.
